In this environment, Nord argues investors want to take risk but face a valuation challenge — hybrid capital allows investors to remain invested and take risk in a more defensive way, without maxing out leverage or accepting full equity exposure at stretched valuations. This underpins Apollo's view that hybrid is well-suited to the current macro backdrop.
quote: If you listen to Torsten's recent mid-year outlook, we're still in a performing economy. He's still constructed on growth. He would assign low probability of a recession coming up here. And so I think investors want to take risk in an environment like that one. The challenge is really on the valuation side. And so how do you think, how as an investor can you put risk assets into your portfolio and feel like you're coming in at a point of value? That's where this maybe really is. You want to stay invested, but maybe you want to stay invested in a more defensive way.
episode_title: Hybrid: Rethinking Risk and Return

headline: Apollo provided hybrid structured capital to Expedia during COVID to meet liquidity needs as an example of creative capital structuring
reasoning: Nord uses Expedia as a specific example of a hybrid transaction where the company needed liquidity during COVID but did not want incremental debt (which affects leverage profile and ratings) and did not want to give up equity control via a PE solution. This illustrates Apollo's core thesis that hybrid capital can fill the gap between pure debt and pure equity when neither is optimal for the counterparty.

Or maybe it's a structured equity investment in someone else's continuation vehicle. Or maybe it's an example of debt, where we're buying debt, and then we have some equity too... headline: Slok recommends value and earnings-quality equities — particularly large caps — as higher debt servicing costs penalise unprofitable companies in both public and private equity

headline: Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok sees strong US growth in H2 2026 driven by three concurrent tailwinds: AI boom, industrial renaissance, and the One Big Beautiful Bill

Together these push growth well above the long-run 2% trend, raising the risk of overheating rather than stagflation despite Middle East geopolitical tensions.

The data center build out is helpful. The energy build out is very helpful for growth. And we also at the same time have the industrial renaissance, which is also helpful for growth. And we also third and finally also have the one big bill for bill, which is also helpful for growth. So we're having a number of factors that are quite unique.

headline: Slok views AI data center and compute infrastructure as a multi-decade 'picks and shovels' opportunity unlikely to slow regardless of who captures AI value

So as a result of that, there will be huge demand for data centers, there will be huge demand for compute for the next 5, 10, 20 years, and that is the parallel to the picks and shovels, to the gold rush, namely that those investments in infrastructure and services that provide the basic core highway for AI is likely going to be the more interesting parts from an investing perspective.
episode_title: Torsten Slok’s Mid-Year Outlook: Three Forces Driving Markets

headline: Forward rate curve flattening and rate cuts coming off the table means real estate returns must now be driven by income and operational alpha rather than cap rate compression.
reasoning: The two-decade bull market in interest rates acted as a consistent tailwind for real estate values via cap rate compression. With the forward curve flattening and rate cut expectations being removed from consensus, real estate investors must return to fundamental income generation and operational value creation. This shifts the competitive advantage toward managers with genuine operational capabilities rather than financial engineering.
